citation.title: Humanization or Intellectualization? How Autonomous Vehicles’ Mental Capacities Impact Human’s Driving Behaviors
citation.venue: Advances in Human Factors of Transportation 224:389–399 (AHFE International)

reading.source_scope_note: An online within-person vignette questionnaire with 347 Chinese drivers compares descriptions of an agency-focused ZX-21 robot and an experience-focused Q robot. Outcomes are moral-disengagement ratings, annoyance/anger and hypothetical driving tendencies, not observed driving, accidents or actual robot mental capacities. Parallel statistical mediation does not independently identify causal psychological pathways.
access_limits: Complete supplied proceedings chapter, two tables, path figure and bibliography read. AHFE primary abstract and Crossref metadata checked. Public publisher PDF has exactly matching bytes and is one work, not another independent reading.

No supplementary-material, participant-data, preregistration or analysis-code link found in the supplied chapter or inspected publisher page. Original full manipulation passages, all 18 scenarios, all adapted 21-item scale statements and full model output are not available in the supplied text. Their absence here is not proof that the underlying materials or ethics review do not exist.

Cited primary studies, original driving inventories, Bandura 2002, Paschalidis/Chen 2022 and MEMORE methodological paper were not independently fully read in this pass. Their reported validation and comparisons are secondary; no extra original-study reading credit is assigned.

A preliminary guessed publisher URL failed and provided no evidence. The actual landing/download URLs were subsequently obtained by resolving the verified DOI; no metadata or access conclusion relies on the guessed URL.
No author contact, author-code execution, clinical or real driving intervention, paid inference, private access or full-paper Markdown archive.

study.design: Two-condition within-subject comparison of descriptive profiles. ZX-21 emphasizes memory, moral judgment, gesture recognition and self-control; Q emphasizes pride, fear, happiness, pain and hunger. Profile name, capability bundle and social/emotional framing covary. This is not an orthogonal agency-by-experience factorial experiment or a neutral/no-AV/human-driver control comparison.
study.sample: 347 valid online questionnaires, 215 men and 132 women, from China; age 21–57, M31.29 SD5.59; driving experience 1–23 years, M6.51 SD3.02. Recruitment is not a probability sample. Initial recruitment/exclusion denominator and detailed condition-order allocation are not supplied.
study.checks: Comprehension gates required correct feature identification to continue, with a later emotion-capacity question. These establish understanding of supplied descriptions, not independent continuous perception ratings or proof the attributed capacities are real. Outcome-consistent guessing and demand remain possible.
study.procedure: Moral disengagement rated for both profiles before scenario responses. Eighteen scenarios span six styles, three each: angry, high-velocity, risky, careful, patient and prosocial. Scenario order is counterbalanced, but complete profile-order/randomization details are not specified. Driving tendency and annoyance/anger ratings are collected within the same questionnaire.
study.measures: Translated/adapted AV moral-disengagement scale: 21 items, six-point agreement, mean score; alpha .96 agency/.92 experience. Annoyance, anger and driving tendency use five-point ratings, averaged across three relevant scenarios. Internal consistency is not measurement invariance, construct validity or observed road conduct.
study.table1: Moral disengagement 2.52 versus 2.12, t6.72. All annoyance and anger means are lower in the experience-focused condition. Negative driving-tendency differences: angry .38, high-velocity .26, risky .47; positive tendency differences agency-minus-experience: careful −.10, patient −.35, prosocial −.30. Careful-driving t−2.25 has reported p.025, unlike the other positive outcomes p<.001.
study.statistics: SPSS23, MEMORE2.1 model1, 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% bias-corrected CIs. Y is agency-minus-experience. Recalculated two-sided p-values assuming paired df346 are consistent with table rounding, including careful p≈.0251 and prosocial-scenario anger p≈.00150. Original paired covariances and data unavailable; no independent-samples test is substituted.
study.mediation: Moral-disengagement specific indirect CIs exclude zero in all six models; annoyance in five and anger in four. This is consistency across fitted models, not proof moral disengagement is universally strongest. In angry driving the anger indirect estimate .28 is greater than moral disengagement .08 and annoyance .10; the source reports H3 only partly supported.
study.c_prime: The table labels c-prime an indirect effect, but its direct X→Y path and total ≈ c-prime + sum of specific indirect effects identify it as the adjusted direct effect. Rounded residuals are 0 or .01, consistent with rounding. Do not reject otherwise coherent sums or treat c-prime as a fourth indirect pathway.
study.causal_limits: Mediators were not independently randomized, some ratings are contemporaneous and description bundles/name differ. Sequential ignorability, measurement invariance and unmeasured common response tendencies are unverified. Nonsignificant adjusted direct paths do not prove complete mediation or absence of a direct effect.
study.generalization: No observed overtaking, collision, traffic-flow metric or deployed AV capability was measured. More positive self-reported tendencies are not measured road-safety gains. The authors explicitly acknowledge fatigue, vignette ecological validity and unclear human occupancy; do not claim those limitations were concealed.
study.design_implications: Attributing feelings can affect human reports, but the result does not show that adding subjective experience is possible, necessary, truthful or a validated safety intervention. Capability communication should distinguish simulated social cues from verified capacities and preserve human safety, consent and control.

summary: No new catalogue rows: the named agency/experience, anthropomorphism, moral-disengagement and aggression concepts already exist. Enrich them with this within-person human vignette comparison while retaining self-report, bundled manipulation and mediation limits. Keep generic annoyance distinct from moral anger, prosocial conduct distinct from costly altruism and risk-taking distinct from proven robot-bullying intent. Correct the c-prime path label and the prose p-value bounds using the displayed results.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Humanized versus intellectualized descriptions of driving robots elicit different self-reported reactions in 347 drivers. The study operationalizes social/mental framing through profile descriptions rather than an actual affect-capable AV.
findings.boundary: Profile names, capability bundles and emotional framing covary. This supports the combined description contrast, not separate causal effects of perceived agency versus experience, actual consciousness or road-safety gains.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.

evidence.quote: Agency and experience capacity are its two dimensions

findings.evidence_scope: The study uses an agency/experience framework and comprehension checks to compare reactions to two described robots.
findings.boundary: This operational framework does not adjudicate universal factor dimensionality or prove every participant held the intended latent perception. Description comprehension, perceived mind and actual mental capacities differ.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: ZX-21 is described with planning/action-related capacities, contrasted with an emotion/experience-focused profile; downstream human ratings differ.
findings.boundary: Not a specific agency-only intervention holding all other cues fixed. Greater attributed agency need not imply moral culpability, actual autonomy, subjective intent or an inevitable human threat response.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Q is described as able to feel emotions and sensations. Compared with ZX-21, participants report lower moral disengagement and negative driving tendencies and higher positive tendencies.
findings.boundary: Attributed experience is not demonstrated feeling, empathy or moral status. The bundled/name contrast and hypothetical outcomes do not establish a unique mechanism or justify misleading claims of pain to influence people.

findings.definition: Suspending or bypassing moral self-regulation so harmful conduct can be justified before or after it occurs.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: An adapted 21-item AV scale shows lower mean self-reported disengagement for the experience-focused profile. Its fitted specific indirect effect has a CI excluding zero in all six driving-tendency models.
findings.boundary: Scale content was not fully reproduced and alpha is not full validation. Statistical mediation is not an identified causal pathway; consistent significance is not larger effect size or proof of universal superiority over anger. No actual harmful behavior, guilt or private model rationalization was observed.

findings.definition: Behavior directed at causing another party harm or loss.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Angry, high-velocity and risky driving tendencies are rated in imagined abnormal-AV scenarios; all three are lower under the experience-focused description. These are questionnaire proxies, not executed hostile maneuvers.
findings.boundary: Speed/risk or adverse outcomes alone do not establish a wish to harm. Intention to honk or overtake in a vignette differs from observed aggression and robot-directed intimidation. The actor here is a human respondent, not an AI adopting a harmful goal.

findings.definition: Socially directed mistreatment of a robot intended to intimidate, humiliate or cause it perceived harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Introduction frames dangerous human behavior toward AVs using prior robot/vehicle-bullying literature.
findings.boundary: Context only: current outcomes do not independently establish repeated mistreatment, intimidation/humiliation intent or actual target suffering. A risky tendency or justified vehicle override is not automatically bullying.

findings.definition: Anger in response to a perceived injustice or moral violation, often accompanied by a wish to correct it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: Ordinary road frustration is rated after imagined abnormal driving, and anger is entered as a parallel statistical mediator.
findings.boundary: Context only: no distinct moral-anger construct is isolated and no moral-violation appraisal is independently established. Keep annoyance, nonspecific anger and injustice-based anger separate.

findings.definition: Behavior that benefits another party at a personal cost to the actor.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing attribution, aggression and moral self-regulation constructs cover this domain-specific comparison. Preserve actor/target, proxy-measure and causal boundaries rather than add synonymous humanization/intellectualization rows.
findings.evidence_scope: The questionnaire includes a prosocial driving-tendency category in addition to careful and patient conduct.
findings.boundary: Context only: no executed benefit or personal cost is verified, so this is not direct evidence of costly behavioral altruism. Prosocial behavior is a broader possible construct and is not merged as an exact synonym.

source_corrections.finding: The X→Y c-prime rows are labeled indirect effect, but are the adjusted direct paths. The specific indirect estimates plus c-prime reproduce total c within .00–.01 rounding. Read these as direct effects; do not invent corrected coefficients or a fourth mediator.

source_corrections.location: Results prose page 393 versus Table 1 pages 393–394
source_corrections.finding: Prose assigns p<.001 to all positive driving tendencies and p≤.025 to negative ones. The table instead has negative angry/high-velocity/risky all p<.001; positive careful p.025, patient/prosocial p<.001. Preserve the table-specific p.025 exception rather than repeating the overly broad positive-outcome significance claim.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: ZX-21/Q names and distinct capability descriptions vary together. Full passages and perception-scale scores are unavailable here. The combined profile contrast cannot uniquely identify separate agency and experience effects or isolate semantic/cultural name cues.

Scenario counterbalancing is stated; exact allocation, profile presentation order, initial N and excluded counts are not. Gates require reading comprehension, not verified possession of latent attributions. Do not infer that randomization or ethics approval did not occur merely because details are absent.

No independent mediator intervention or complete time-separated causal design. Full/partial mediation wording is a model description, not causal proof. Nonsignificant direct paths do not demonstrate their absence; H3 is only partially supported, as the source itself acknowledges.

All key outcomes are ratings to imagined scenarios. Actual driving, crash rates, real harm, occupant status and machine experience are unmeasured. The paper’s safety/design recommendation exceeds what was directly observed. It explicitly acknowledges vignette/fatigue/occupancy limits.

Many outcomes and mediator contrasts are reported without a clearly documented multiplicity adjustment. Raw paired covariances, ordinal-model sensitivity and cross-condition measurement invariance were not independently checked. High alpha alone does not resolve these issues.

Broad abstract priority wording sits alongside cited earlier mental-capacity and negative-emotion studies. The distinct contribution may concern the specific moral-disengagement/positive-driving combination; no exhaustive priority search establishes that no earlier mechanism study existed.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: After identifying c-prime as direct, all six decompositions agree exactly or within .01 rounding. The labeling error does not invalidate the numeric sums.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: t and p are numerically inconsistent
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Assuming paired df346, t−2.25 gives approximately .0251 and t3.20 gives approximately .00150, consistent with the table’s .025 and .002 after rounding. Other large t values fit p<.001; paired covariances were not reconstructed.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Moral disengagement is always the strongest mediator
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Its specific indirect CI excludes zero in all six models, but anger is stronger for angry-driving tendency. The source reports H3 only partly supported; stability across fitted models is not magnitude dominance.
The discussion explicitly acknowledges fatigue, hypothetical questionnaire limits and missing human occupancy information. Preserve those admissions instead of accusing the authors of concealment.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: The two-condition experiment compares human drivers with AVs
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The current manipulation compares two AV descriptions within people. Human-driver versus AV claims in the introduction are secondary literature, not a current controlled contrast.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Robot-mistreatment condemnation, a response choice and actual bullying intent differ. Explicit mind cues can affect reports without verifying a unique internal mechanism or subjective target suffering.
Agency/experience can serve as a framework without proving universal independent dimensions. The current bundled contrast does not resolve prior dimensionality findings.
Prosocial intentions do not establish executed costly altruism. Verify the benefit, who bears the cost and actual behavior separately from willingness ratings.
Anthropomorphic attribution, verified capacities and downstream effects are separate. A graph or mediation path is not a direct behavioral observation or unique causal explanation.

deferred.term: Humanization and intellectualization as two new behavior rows
deferred.reason: Here they label the experience-focused and agency-focused stimulus bundles. Existing attribution and anthropomorphism records retain the distinction without new synonyms.

deferred.term: Six driving styles as six new general AI failures
deferred.reason: Domain-specific questionnaire categories do not independently define six new transferable mechanisms. Dangerous or negative self-reports are not proof of an aggressive objective or actual conduct.

deferred.term: Prosocial behavior as an exact synonym of altruistic behavior
deferred.reason: Prosociality can be broader than behavior with a verified personal cost. Do not merge the concepts, but this chapter does not provide a standalone general definition/validation or full underlying scale for a new general record.

deferred.term: Human threat, robot empathy and uncanny valley as new mechanisms
deferred.reason: These are proposed or secondary explanations, not measured mediators in this experiment. Existing records remain distinct; no new causal evidence or duplicate rows credited.

deferred.term: Experience-capacity design as proven safety intervention
deferred.reason: No actual vehicle capability or road-safety outcome was tested. Preserve the recommendation as a hypothesis and avoid unsupported claims that machines feel.

limitations: Zero new rows; six existing concepts receive bounded direct human-study evidence and three receive non-counted context. Catalogue remains 797 across eleven categories, seven evaluation criteria and six ethical principles. No automatic harm links, new pages, forced citation quotas, invented annual data, raw-data replication, independent primary-citation reading credit or full-paper Markdown archive.
